rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. A usable word entry  ·  A useful vocabulary note has the word, its word class, a short definition, and one sentence of your own. Three different sentences fix a meaning better than a synonym list alone.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Trick 1: Word-formation questions: prefix/suffix changes part of speech — 'happy (adj) → happiness (noun) → happily (adv)'; identify the base word first.  ·  Trick 2: Context-clue method for unseen vocabulary: definition, example, contrast (but/however), and cause signals around the unknown word give the meaning without a dictionary.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Roots, prefixes, and suffixes  ·  A root carries the core meaning, as port means carry. A prefix changes that meaning, as in transport and export. A suffix often changes the word class, as in create, creation, and creative. Check a dictionary after the first guess.  ·  ### 3. Collocation

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Trick 3: Synonym questions: check the word's PART OF SPEECH in the sentence first — a synonym must match both meaning AND word class.  ·  define + example each sub-idea: vocabulary building.  ·  one worked example for "Vocabulary Building" — check units / edge cases.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: recall card: definition → formula → limit → one error to avoid.  ·  State the limit / condition where a formula or rule stops being valid before applying it.  ·  Collocations are words that habitually go together: make a decision, do homework, strong tea, heavy rain. A sentence can be grammatical and still sound wrong if the pairing is off, as in do a decision.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ### 4. Context clues  ·  In a passage, a definition may follow that is or a dash. An example after such as narrows the meaning. A contrast after but or unlike tells you what the word is not.  ·  ### 5. Register

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Register is how formal a word is. Kids and children, buy and purchase, ask and request can share a meaning and differ in tone. Match the word to the reader: a letter to a principal is more formal than a note to a friend.  ·  # Vocabulary Building ## 1.
